newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Shenzhen shares close limits-down on crackdown.
newsitem.headline: Shenzhen shares close limits-down on crackdown.

text.p: Shenzhen's B share index plunged 14.93 points, or a limit-down of 10 percent, to 134.43 points on Monday after Beijing unexpectedLY announced a crackdown on the stock markets, traders said.
The A share index also closed limit-down of 10 percent, losing 46.34 points to 417.2 points.
Traders said nearly all Shenzhen-listed A and B shares hit the new 10-percent limit-down a few seconds after the opening.

The People's Daily, mouthpiece of the Communist Party, said on Monday that the country's two stock markets in Shenzhnn and Shanghai were overheating due to speculative trading and warned of a crash similar to the great Wall Street collapse of 1929.

Last Friday, the Shenzhen and Shanghai bourses announced that they were imposing a limit of 10 percent on daily movements for individual stocks with effect from Monday to stop extraordinary price movements.

On Sunday, the China Securities Regulatory Commission, the country's top securities watchdog, announced a quota of 10 billion yuan worth of share issues for 1996 for use in 1997, doubling the 1995 quota of 5.5 billion yuan used this year.
Brokers said this appeared to be an apparent bid to cap rises in share prices by accelerating the pace of market expansion.
Local brokers said most Shenzhen-listed stocks are likely to register limit-down closes over the next few sessions as investors have been intimidated by the People's Daily commentary.
"Few people would dare to build positions at this time and the number of sellers is seen increasing," one broker said.

"Panic selling emerged immediately after the opening and pushed almost all stocks down to their 10 percent limit, with a large number of selling orders unable to be processed because of few buyers," he said.
B share turnover plunged to HK15.48 million, compared with last Friday's HK$432.45 million. A share turnover fell to 693.64 million yuan from 9.26 billion yuan on Friday.
Traders said the A markets would be most affected in the short term because they have risen more in the past few months.
